subject: ss-critical-care
title: Infections and antimicrobials in the ICU

steps.tx: Ventilator-associated pneumonia (**VAP**) is pneumonia arising more than 48 hours after starting mechanical ventilation. Its pathogenesis follows a sequence: oropharyngeal colonisation by potential pathogens, aspiration of colonised secretions, and compromise of host defences. Antibiotic exposure is the dominant driver of replacement of commensal flora by resistant organisms. Endotracheal tube **biofilm** shelters bacteria from both antibiotics and immune cells, which explains recurrence with the same strain.

steps.tx: Carbapenem-resistant **Acinetobacter baumannii** is a major ICU pathogen, with crude mortality reaching up to 70 percent in bacteraemia. Resistance is mostly mediated by Ambler class D oxacillinases. The abaI quorum-sensing gene drives biofilm on devices. For carbapenem-resistant isolates, combination therapy with a polymyxin and a sulbactam-containing agent is favoured. Empirical choice is unreliable without local susceptibility data.

steps.tx: Carbapenem-resistant **Enterobacterales** most often resist carbapenems through carbapenemase enzymes, which hydrolyse carbapenems. Polymyxins are reserved for confirmed carbapenem-resistant organisms rather than used empirically. Colistin and polymyxin B cause dose-limiting **nephrotoxicity** and neurotoxicity, so renal function and drug levels need monitoring. Aminoglycosides must not be the sole anti-pseudomonal agent in pneumonia.

steps.tx: Reassess **empirical antibiotics** at 48 to 72 hours. Clinical improvement and negative cultures allow **de-escalation** to a narrower agent. A falling **procalcitonin** can support early stopping, but it must never override treatment of a clinically suspected pneumonia. For pneumonia with a good response, a seven day course is standard. For MRSA ventilator associated pneumonia, older practice aimed for a **vancomycin trough** of 15 to 20 mg/L, whereas **AUC guided dosing** is increasingly preferred.

steps.tx: Invasive candidiasis and **Clostridioides difficile** complicate ICU care. Central line associated bloodstream infection (**CLABSI**) and catheter associated urinary tract infection (CAUTI) are device-related infections needing line removal and culture-guided therapy. Indian practice under ICMR and NMC frameworks emphasises local antibiogram use, while US IDSA guidance is similar on reassessment. Augmented renal clearance may need higher beta-lactam doses, and therapeutic drug monitoring guides aminoglycosides and vancomycin.
